# Is there a scientific method? {#sec-session-01}

**Meeting 1 of 13**

## Central question

Is hypothesis-testing a universal account of inquiry, a standard for justification, or one useful mode among several?

## The paper pair

Every citation on this page links to its full record in the [bibliography](../bibliography.qmd), which also lists this meeting's readings with access notes.

**Pairing type:** Methodological ideal / evidential counterpoint.

Platt, J. R. (1964). Strong Inference. *Science, 146*(3642), 347–353. [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347](<https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347>)

Read Platt in full. Identify the role of alternative explanations and discriminating observations.

Cleland, C. E. (2001). Historical science, experimental science, and the scientific method. *Geology, 29*(11), 987–990. [https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2](<https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2>)

Read Cleland’s Geology paper in full. It makes the argument in four pages, for geologists; the discussant brings the rest.

### Why these papers belong together

Platt offers a prescriptive strategy; Cleland analyzes differences between experimental interventions and reconstructing past events. Neither paper directly records this group’s daily research. Test both against an actual project rather than declaring one a complete scientific method. [@platt1964; @cleland2001]

### Discussant-led paper

One rotating discussant takes the following in depth and brings its argument into the discussion; everyone else reads the abstract.

Cleland, C. E. (2002). Methodological and Epistemic Differences between Historical Science and Experimental Science. *Philosophy of Science, 69*(3), 474–496. [https://doi.org/10.1086/342455](<https://doi.org/10.1086/342455>)

The full version of the Geology paper above: the time asymmetry that makes trace-hunting a rational strategy rather than a consolation prize, the "smoking gun", and the reply to the charge that historical science is epistemically inferior. The discussant brings what the four-page version leaves out. [@cleland2002]

### Reading notes

The convenor's notes from the two assigned papers, offered as a starting point rather than a summary of the discussion. They bear on discussion question 3 below, on whether the papers describe how ideas are generated or how claims are warranted, and the diagram is the loop the case exercise compares a real project against. #### Inference, deduction, and hypothesis generation

Deduction is not the opposite of inference. It is one kind of inference. Platt's workflow embeds deductive reasoning inside a broader process of inductive inference.

| Term | Definition | Role in strong inference |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Inference** | Any reasoned movement from premises or evidence to a conclusion. | The general category containing deduction, induction, and other forms of reasoning. |
| **Deduction** | Reasoning in which the conclusion must follow if the premises are true. | Derives a predicted observation from each hypothesis: if $H_i$ and its auxiliary assumptions hold, then $P_i$ should occur. |
| **Inductive inference** | Reasoning from observations to a broader but provisional conclusion. New evidence can revise it. | Uses the observed outcome to exclude, retain, or refine hypotheses. This is what Platt calls the branching logical tree [@platt1964, p. 347]. |
| **Hypothesis generation** | The creative proposal of possible explanations, sometimes called abduction. | Produces the alternatives at the beginning of each cycle. Platt says this step requires "intellectual inventions, which must be cleverly chosen" rather than a mechanical rule, and sends the reader to Pólya for how to make them [@platt1964, p. 347]. |

**The logic within one branch.** For a candidate hypothesis $H_i$, together with auxiliary assumptions $A$:

$$H_i + A \Rightarrow P_i$$

This movement from hypothesis to prediction is **deduction**.

If the experiment instead produces $\neg P_i$, then:

$$\neg P_i \Rightarrow \neg(H_i + A)$$

This is the basis of **exclusion**. Strictly speaking, the test has contradicted the combination of the hypothesis and its assumptions, not the hypothesis alone. Platt does not draw that distinction; Cleland makes it the center of her case against falsificationism, with the astronomers who kept Newton and rejected an auxiliary assumption to find Neptune as the example [@cleland2001, p. 988].

The resulting revision of the hypothesis set is **inductive inference**:

$$\{H_1, H_2, H_3\} + \text{observed outcome} \Rightarrow \text{a smaller, provisionally preferred set}$$

Observing $P_i$ does **not** deductively prove $H_i$, because another hypothesis might also predict $P_i$. Strong inference addresses this problem by seeking observations for which the competing hypotheses make different predictions.

#### Platt's branching discipline: strong inference

Platt's strong inference is a repeating process of generating alternatives, designing an observation that distinguishes them, excluding incompatible alternatives, and refining what remains [@platt1964, p. 347].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-strong-inference
%%| fig-cap: "Platt's strong inference as a branching loop. Each cycle generates alternatives, deduces predictions that differ between them, runs the experiment, excludes what the outcome rules out, and refines what remains. The hypotheses are contrasted, never proved."
%%{init: {"theme": "base", "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "18px", "fontFamily": "Source Serif 4, Georgia, serif", "primaryColor": "#e7f0f2", "primaryBorderColor": "#1c6a7f", "primaryTextColor": "#153742", "lineColor": "#49616a", "secondaryColor": "#ffffff", "tertiaryColor": "#f5f4f2", "edgeLabelBackground": "#f5f4f2"}, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true, "nodeSpacing": 28, "rankSpacing": 42, "curve": "basis", "padding": 10}}}%%
flowchart TD
    Q["Problem or<br/>scientific question"] --> A["1. Devise alternative<br/>hypotheses"]

    A --> H1["Hypothesis H1"]
    A --> H2["Hypothesis H2"]
    A --> H3["Hypothesis H3"]

    H1 & H2 & H3 --> P["2. Deduce contrasting predictions<br/>and devise a crucial experiment"]

    P --> T["3. Carry out the experiment<br/>to obtain a clean result"]
    T --> O{"Observed outcome:<br/>nature chooses a branch"}

    O -- "Outcome A" --> OA["Exclude H2 and H3;<br/>H1 remains"]
    O -- "Outcome B" --> OB["Exclude H1 and H3;<br/>H2 remains"]
    O -- "Outcome C" --> OC["Exclude H1 and H2;<br/>H3 remains"]
    O -- "No clear<br/>separation" --> NC["No secure exclusion:<br/>recheck or redesign the test"]

    OA & OB & OC --> R["1'. Refine the remaining possibility<br/>into sequential hypotheses<br/>or subhypotheses"]
    NC --> P
    R --> P

    classDef step fill:#e7f0f2,stroke:#1c6a7f,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#153742;
    classDef hyp fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1c6a7f,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#153742;
    classDef branch fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1c6a7f,stroke-width:2px,color:#153742;
    classDef warn fill:#f6e9e2,stroke:#a1512b,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#5a2e17;
    class Q,A,P,T,R step;
    class H1,H2,H3,OA,OB,OC hyp;
    class O branch;
    class NC warn;
```

> **Exclusion** means that an observed outcome is incompatible with a prediction required by one or more hypotheses. Those hypotheses are removed from the current candidate set. The hypothesis that remains has survived this test; it has not been proved true.

The ideal experiment is therefore not merely one that produces information. It is one for which the possible outcomes change which explanations remain viable.

**Is it Baconian?** Platt says so himself. He traces the "conditional inductive tree" to Bacon's *Novum Organum*, with its "Instances of the Fingerpost" that mark where roads part and its rule that induction must proceed by "proper rejections and exclusions" [@platt1964, p. 349], and he presents Chamberlin's multiple working hypotheses as the second invention "needed to round out the Baconian scheme" [@platt1964, p. 350; @chamberlin1965]. In today's vocabulary the exclusion step is eliminative induction, and Platt quotes Popper for the claim that science advances only by disproofs [@platt1964, p. 350]. Two things in the diagram are not Baconian and not in Platt. The distinction between $H_i$ and $A$ above the exclusion arrow is Cleland's [@cleland2001, p. 988]. And the box that generates $H_1$, $H_2$, $H_3$ has no rule inside it; Platt concedes as much, and the seminar's question is what happens there.

## Prepare before the meeting

Read the [glossary](../glossary.qmd) and bring one definition you would change, with the paper of your own that it fails on. Bring one important paper and a short reconstruction of how the work actually proceeded. Mark which steps are documented and which are inferred.

## Discussion questions

1. Can an observational study discriminate hypotheses without controlling the system?
2. Which research actions are not well described as a test?
3. Are we describing how ideas are generated or how claims are warranted?

### Case exercise

Reconstruct a project as initial knowledge -> observation -> representation -> question -> proposed explanation -> check. Compare that trajectory with the published narrative, and with Platt's loop in the [reading notes](#reading-notes): where the project left the loop, or never entered it, is the row it contributes to the inquiry-mode ledger. Do not invent a private chronology from the article structure.

### Definitions to fix in this meeting

Five terms that the rest of the quarter measures need a first working definition today, so that meetings 10 to 12 and the [corpus study](../corpus-study.qmd) define their variables before seeing the data rather than after: field-shaping, novelty, depth, interdisciplinarity, and impact. The [glossary](../glossary.qmd) proposes one for each, with the standard measure and what it leaves out. Agree on wording, or record the disagreement and who holds which side. Do not settle whether the measures are valid; that is the work of meetings 10 to 12.

## Agent-design or evaluation output

Inquiry-action vocabulary v1: the [glossary](../glossary.qmd) as amended in this meeting. Its modes of inquiry are the rows of the ledger and the codebook for the corpus study; its terms of assessment are the variables the quarter measures. Note where an agent should abstain or seek more evidence.

## Optional extensions

- @chamberlin1965: [The Method of Multiple Working Hypotheses](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.148.3671.754). Science (1965). Written by a geologist, and the source Platt built on. Chamberlin's target is the single ruling hypothesis; his remedy is to hold a family of them at once. Decide whether Platt's loop and Chamberlin's family are the same practice.
- @simon1973: [Does Scientific Discovery Have a Logic?](https://doi.org/10.1086/288559). Philosophy of Science (1973). Simon argues, against Popper, that discovery is problem solving with describable heuristics. The computer discovery programs listed in [meeting 13](13-agent-design-and-evaluation.qmd) were built on this argument.
- @klahr1988: [Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1201_1). Cognitive Science (1988). People solving a discovery task searched two spaces, one of hypotheses and one of experiments, and some made progress by running experiments with no hypothesis at all. Experimental evidence that inquiry has more than one search mode.
- @holmes1987: [Scientific Writing and Scientific Discovery](https://doi.org/10.1086/354391). Isis (1987). Holmes compared laboratory notebooks with the published papers written from them and describes what the paper leaves out. The basis for standing question 5.

**On geological method in particular.** The pair above is about science in general; these are about how geologists reason, and they are the start of the answer to whether the seminar has yet reached a general geoscience workflow.

- @gilbert1896: [The Origin of Hypotheses, Illustrated by the Discussion of a Topographic Problem](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3.53.1). Science (1896). Grove Karl Gilbert on where a geological hypothesis comes from, worked through his own attempt to explain the Coon Butte crater: by analogy, by enumeration of the possible causes, and by the test that separates them. The geological ancestor of Platt's method, and an account of the generative step Platt hands to Pólya.
- @johnson1933: [Role of Analysis in Scientific Investigation](https://doi.org/10.1130/GSAB-44-461). Geological Society of America Bulletin (1933). A geologist's account of analysis as the method of geological investigation, with the failure modes it guards against.
- @frodeman1995: [Geological reasoning: Geology as an interpretive and historical science](https://doi.org/10.1130/0016-7606(1995)107%3C0960:GRGAAI%3E2.3.CO;2). Geological Society of America Bulletin (1995). Geology as an interpretive and historical science, against the physics model of method. The geological statement of Cleland's thesis, seven years earlier.
- @kleinhans2005: [Terra Incognita: Explanation and Reduction in Earth Science](https://doi.org/10.1080/02698590500462356). International Studies in the Philosophy of Science (2005). What explanation and reduction mean in earth science, where the systems are open and the histories unique.
- @elliott2007: [Revisiting Chamberlin: Multiple Working Hypotheses for the 21st Century](https://doi.org/10.1641/B570708). BioScience (2007). Chamberlin's multiple working hypotheses reconsidered for present-day practice, with the model-selection tools that now implement them.
